newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland leader hopeful on Loyalist truce.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland leader hopeful on Loyalist truce.

text.p: Northern Ireland's key Protestant leader held talks with jailed Loyalists on Friday and said he was confident they wanted supporters outside to stand by a two-year-old guerrilla ceasefire.
"I left the meeting feeling very strongly that the prisoners here wish to see the ceasefire sustained," David Trimble, leader of the pro-British Ulster Unionist party (UUP) said.

Trimble spent more than two hours talking to spokesmen for Loyalist guerrillas jailed at the top-security Maze prison for crimes committed during their 27-year war to avenge IRA violence and to keep Northern Ireland British.

They were instrumental in calling an October 1994 ceasefire which has been under threat since the Catholic-backed Irish Republican Army ended its truce in February and bombed targets in Britain, Germany, and last week, Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters south of Belfast.
"I think the biggest threat to the ceasefire is the IRA," said Trimble, whose UUP party is the most powerful political voice of the 60 percent Protestant majority.
"There is a risk that further Republican violence would destabilise the situation," he told reporters outside the gates of the prison, south of Belfast.
He said that he would be holding talks with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, over Loyalist calls for their prison sentences to be cut to reward them for abiding by the truce.
"I think the question of how the Life Sentences Review Board operates is worth looking at," said Trimble, referring to the state body which oversees the carrying out of jail terms.
Trimble was speaking at the gates of a prison where about 550 prisoners, both Loyalists and Republicans, are held for security offences linked to the 27-year conflict.

Northern Ireland has been tense since the IRA struck army headquarters in Lisburn -- its first attack in the province for two years -- killing a soldier, injuring 20 and raising widespread fears that the province would slide back into the tit-for-tat violence it knew for 27 years.
In Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry, moves were being made behind the scenes to defuse tension over a planned march on Saturday by the Apprentice Boys, a Protestant order, police said.
They said they had not yet decided whether to grant permission to the Order to walk along the city's walls on Saturday morning, a ritual which Catholic residents see as intimidation.

The Bogside residents association, which groups members of the predominantly Catholic community which lives close to the walls, has called for a counter-parade and rally at exactly the same time on Saturday.

The annual march was rerouted in August when sectarian violence erupted across the province over the holding of Protstant parades and the Apprentice Boys vowed at the time that they would parade later.
Martin McGuinnes, a senior member of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein accused the Apprentice Boys of seeking confrontation.
"I feel it will be extremely unfortunate if Apprentice Boys decide to abandon the option of negotiation in favour of confrontation," said McGuinnes, a Londonderry resident.
